![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13979325/assets/e09f5a90c683876f849577cd75af3c77cc21c6f9af10c5a4ece47718aa33f738.png)

The figure above shows the graph of a piecewise linear function $y=f(x).$ The point $A$ has coordinates $(2,4)$ and lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $(4,2)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x),$ what is $({f}^{-1})^{′}(4)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $(4,2)$ lies on ${f}^{-1},$ we have ${f}^{-1}(4)=2.$
The slope of the tangent to $f(x)$ for $x\in [0,4]$ is $-\frac{1}{2}$, hence, ${f}^{′}(2)=-\frac{1}{2}.$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse function is

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Evaluating at $x=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(4) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(4))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(e,1).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x} \\ {f}^{′}(e) & =\frac{1}{e}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(e,1)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(1,e)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(e)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{e})} \\  & =e.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(1,0).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x-1}{{x}^{2}+1} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{(x-1)^{′}\cdot ({x}^{2}+1)-(x-1)\cdot {({x}^{2}+1)}^{′}}{{({x}^{2}+1)}^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1\cdot ({x}^{2}+1)-(x-1)\cdot 2x}{{({x}^{2}+1)}^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}+1-2{x}^{2}+2x}{{({x}^{2}+1)}^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1+2x-{x}^{2}}{{({x}^{2}+1)}^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1+2(1)-{1}^{2}}{{({1}^{2}+1)}^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(1,0)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(0,1)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{3}{2\sqrt{x-3}}$ and the point $P(7,\frac{3}{4})$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ determine the slope of $y={f}^{-1}(x)$ at the point $(\frac{3}{4},7).$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(7,\frac{3}{4}).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3}{2\sqrt{x-3}} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{3}{4(x-3)^{3/2}} \\ {f}^{′}(7) & =-\frac{3}{32}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(7,\frac{3}{4})$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(\frac{3}{4},7)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(\frac{3}{4}) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(\frac{3}{4}))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(7)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-\frac{3}{32})} \\  & =-\frac{32}{3}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Derivative Using Properties of Inverse Functions
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(0),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(0).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(0)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(0) & =x \\ f(x) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,3.\end{aligned}
$$

We discard $x=0$ since the logarithm is not defined here. Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(0)=3.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(3),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2) \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{x-2} \\ {f}^{′}(3) & =2\cdot 3\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-2)+\frac{{3}^{2}}{3-2} \\ {f}^{′}(3) & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\sqrt{2x-1}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(3).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(3),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(3)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(3))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(3).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(3)=x.$ For $x>\frac{1}{2}$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(3) & =x \\ f(x) & =3 \\ \sqrt{2x-1} & =3 \\ 2x-1 & =9 \\ 2x & =10 \\ x & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(5),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\sqrt{2x-1} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-1}} \\ {f}^{′}(5) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\cdot 5-1}} \\ {f}^{′}(5) & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(3) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(3))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(5)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{3})} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)={x}^{3}+5x+2.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(2)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ {x}^{3}+5x+2 & =2 \\ x({x}^{2}+5) & =0 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(2)=0.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{3}+5x+2 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2}+5 \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =3\cdot 0+5 \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(6) & =x \\ f(x) & =6 \\ {4}^{x}+2 & =6 \\ {4}^{x} & =4 \\ {4}^{x} & ={4}^{1} \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(6)=1.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={4}^{x}+2 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={4}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ {f}^{′}(1) & ={4}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ {f}^{′}(1) & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡4\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(6) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(6))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}.\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function Using a Table
canonical_examples.problem:
The following table gives the values of $f(x), f'(x),g(x),$ and $g'(x)$ at some points. Find $(f^{-1}\cdot g)'(1)$ of the product of functions.

| **$x$** | $f(x)$ | $f'(x)$ | $g(x)$ | $g'(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $2$ | $-3$ | $1$ |
| $2$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $3$ | $5$ |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The formula for the derivative of the inverse $f^{-1}(x)$ is

$$
(f^{-1})'(x) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Using this, and the product rule, the derivative of the function $f^{-1}(x)g(x)$ is

$$
(f^{-1}\cdot g)'(x)=\dfrac{g(x)}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}+g'(x)f^{-1}(x).
$$

Substituting $x=1,$ we have

$$
(f^{-1}\cdot g)'(1) =\dfrac{g(1)}{f'(f^{-1}(1))}+g'(1)f^{-1}(1).
$$

From the table, we obtain $f^{-1}(1)=2,$ $g(1)=-3,$ $g'(1)=1,$ and $f'(2)=-1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1}\cdot g)^{′}(1) & =\frac{g(1)}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))}+{g}^{′}(1){f}^{-1}(1) \\  & =\frac{-3}{{f}^{′}(2)}+1\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{-3}{-1}+2 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Consider the function $f(x) =3e^{x}-1.$ Given that $y = f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $(f^{-1})'(2).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To determine $(f^{-1})'(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
\left(f^{-1}\right)'(2) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of $f^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation $f^{-1}(2) = x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ 3{e}^{x}-1 & =2 \\ 3{e}^{x} & =3 \\ {e}^{x} & =1 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f^{-1}(2) = 0.$

Now, we calculate $f'(0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =3{e}^{x}-1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3{e}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =3{e}^{0} \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
